blocks.text: Using microwave equipment with a wavelength of 2.8 cm (Fig 15.6), an interference pattern can be observed. The microwave transmitter is directed at a double gap in a metal barrier. The microwaves are diffracted at the two gaps and spread out into the region beyond, where they are detected with a probe receiver. Moving the probe around finds regions of high intensity (constructive interference) and low intensity (destructive interference). The probe may be connected to a meter, or to an audio amplifier and loudspeaker to give an audible output.

A simple way to show interference of light is to shine a laser through two slits (Fig 15.7): two clear lines on a black slide, separated by a fraction of a millimetre. On the screen a series of equally spaced dots of light, called interference fringes, appears where waves from the two slits arrive in phase (constructive interference); the dark regions between are the result of destructive interference. These bright and dark fringes correspond to the loud and quiet regions of the two loudspeakers.

We can check that light reaches the screen from both slits. Mark a point at a dark fringe, then cover one slit so that light passes through only one. The fringes disappear and a broad band of light, the diffraction pattern of a single slit, appears; the point that was dark is now bright. Covering the other slit instead gives the same effect. So light arrives from both slits, but at the dark fringes the two beams cancel. A bright bulb can give similar results, but a laser is more convenient because its light is concentrated into a narrow, intense beam. Thomas Young had no laser when he first did the experiment in 1801.

blocks.alt: Left: a microwave transmitter faces metal sheets with two gaps; curved wavefronts spread from each gap and overlap; a probe on a stand with a meter finds loud and quiet places. Right: a laser beam passes through a double slit and spreads to a screen, where a column of equally spaced bright red dots appears.
blocks.caption: Demonstrating interference with microwaves and with light (original diagram after Figs 15.6 and 15.7).
blocks.long_description: The same idea works for all waves: two coherent sources a short distance apart give alternate strong and weak regions. Only the scale changes: centimetres for microwaves, fractions of a millimetre for light.

blocks.prompt: Compare the double-slit arrangements for light and for sound waves.
blocks.explanation: Similar: two coherent sources from one generator, and a pattern of strong and weak regions where path differences are whole or half wavelengths. Different: sound uses loudspeakers or gaps metres or centimetres apart, detected by ear or microphone, because its wavelength is long; light needs slits a fraction of a millimetre apart and a screen, because its wavelength is very short.

items: Microwaves (2.8 cm) through two gaps: probe finds strong and weak regions.
Laser through a double slit: equally spaced bright fringes.
Covering one slit removes the fringes: light comes from both slits.
